kjv-italics-revision.response: Stan Spencer, of the Interpreter Foundation, accepts the pattern. He argues that Joseph Smith could see the italics on the page. As an untrained reader he treated them as the weakest part of the verse, and revised around them while dictating. On that view a revealed translation would naturally target exactly those words. FAIR makes a similar case: the italics marked genuinely softer text, so a prophetic revision would land there.
kjv-italics-revision.rationale: Both sides now agree on the fact. The differences cluster on the italics — a typographic feature of one printed English Bible from 1611. That is not in dispute any more. What the defense offers is a reframe, not a denial, and the reframe concedes the thing that matters: he was working from a King James Bible. One problem is left unanswered. In several places, dropping the italic word damages the sense against the Hebrew. A revision guided by God would not be expected to do that.

deutero-isaiah-problem.response: Two lines of answer, and they pull in opposite directions. Kevin Barney and FAIR accept the scholarly dating. They suggest the material entered during translation — Joseph rendering Nephite ideas in the King James Isaiah his readers knew. Other defenders reject the dating instead. They argue for one author, or for an early core of Isaiah 40-55 that could have existed by 600 BC, and point out that late-dating Isaiah partly assumes prophecy cannot predict.
deutero-isaiah-problem.rationale: The exile dating of Isaiah 40-55 is one of the firmest conclusions in Hebrew Bible scholarship, and trained Latter-day Saint scholars accept it — David Bokovoy among them. So the defenses have to pick. Reject the consensus, which is a large thing to do. Or accept it and move the material into the translation — which concedes that the plates could not have held it. That second answer costs a lot, because Abinadi's whole sermon is built on Isaiah 53.

another-gospel-canon-closure.response: Three replies, and the first two are strong. Revelation 22:18 warns against tampering with "the words of the prophecy of this book" — Revelation itself. That was a standard closing curse on a single ancient scroll. Revelation was not even the last book written, and the same logic applied to Deuteronomy 4:2 would cancel everything after Deuteronomy. Many evangelical scholars agree. Second, the warning is about men adding to scripture, not God speaking again. Third, Galatians 1:8 condemns a different gospel — and Latter-day Saints hold that the Book of Mormon teaches the same Christ crucified. On their reading the argument assumes what it is trying to prove.
another-gospel-canon-closure.rationale: The Revelation 22:18 version is the weakest form of this argument and Christians should stop using it. Most textual scholars agree the curse is scoped to Revelation, and the Deuteronomy comparison lands. The Galatians 1:8 form survives that reply, but it does not settle anything by itself. It turns entirely on whether the gospel content actually matches — which sends you to the specific doctrinal cases, on grace and on exaltation. Not a standalone argument. Not answered either.

grace-after-all-we-can-do.response: Four replies. Stephen Robinson of BYU and Royal Skousen read "after all we can do" as an old turn of phrase meaning in spite of all we can do — grace saves despite our failure, not after our success. In 2015 Dieter Uchtdorf of the First Presidency preached that "after" does not mean "because," and that salvation is not earned by hitting a quota. Third, in context Nephi's point is that the law of Moses is dead and only grace saves. Fourth, John Welch reads the verse against the covenant framing of Mosiah 4.
grace-after-all-we-can-do.rationale: The "in spite of" reading is linguistically possible, and after Uchtdorf it is close to official. That genuinely narrows the gap, and Christians who ignore it are arguing with a position the church no longer holds. Two things keep the criticism alive. The reinterpretation is late — from Joseph Fielding Smith through Kimball and McConkie, the standard reading was conditional. And Moroni 10:32 is conditional in its grammar in a way no idiom fixes: deny yourselves of all ungodliness, then is his grace sufficient. Neither side lands a knockout.

trinitarian-monotheism-1830.response: David Paulsen and Ari Bruening of BYU argue the 1830 text is not modalist when read whole. It does tell Father and Son apart — the Father's voice introduces the Son in 3 Nephi 11, and Christ prays to the Father. So its "one God" language describes a unity of distinct persons, no further from later teaching than the New Testament's own "one God" texts are from Nicaea. Mosiah 15 is explained by divine investiture: Christ acts as Father by creation and covenant, and as Son in the flesh — the First Presidency set that out in 1916. Brant Gardner adds that apparent modalism may reflect the limits of translation language.
trinitarian-monotheism-1830.rationale: The narrow charge of modalism is genuinely arguable, and critics do sometimes overstate it — Paulsen really does find Father-Son distinction in the text. The broader point survives anyway. The Book of Mormon insists on one eternal God and says nothing at all about a plurality of gods, eternal progression, God having a body, or humans becoming gods. Those are the doctrines that define mature Mormonism, and the 1830 book is silent on every one. The 1916 divine-investiture apparatus exists precisely because the plain text does not teach the later doctrine.

1837-son-of-edits.response: Three replies. FAIR argues a translator may clarify his own work, and Royal Skousen's critical text project treats the change as clarification. Both readings are defensible, they say, because Christ is called Eternal Father elsewhere in the book — at Mosiah 16:15 — and other such verses were left untouched, which a systematic cover-up would not do. Second, the phrase "mother of God" drew Catholic-sounding objections from Alexander Campbell, so removing it took away a stumbling block without changing doctrine. Third, thousands of changes across editions are typographical, and these four are published openly in Skousen's variant lists.
1837-son-of-edits.rationale: Nobody disputes the facts. FAIR concedes the four insertions and that Joseph Smith made them. Only the meaning is argued. The point that similar language survives elsewhere is fair, and it does weaken a cover-up framing. What no Latter-day Saint source explains well is why a translation given by God needed christological amendment at exactly the verses a critic had attacked, in exactly the years when Smith's teaching about God was shifting. As evidence of a text that changed with its author, this stands. As proof of wholesale rewriting, it overreaches.

jacob-polygamy-vs-dc132.response: FAIR reads Jacob 2:30 as an exception clause. Monogamy is the rule — but "if I will, saith the Lord of Hosts, raise up seed unto me, I will command my people." On that reading D&C 132 is the commanded exception, and the two texts state one coherent policy. On David and Solomon they draw a line: Jacob condemns the unauthorised excess, the Bathsheba affair and the foreign idolatrous wives, while D&C 132:38-39 says David sinned only in the case of Uriah. The wives "given of me" were the authorised ones — and 2 Samuel 12:8 does have Nathan say God gave David his master's wives.
jacob-polygamy-vs-dc132.rationale: The harmonisation is available in the text. 2 Samuel 12:8 really does say that, and Jacob 2:30 can be read as an exception — though some scholars, including Latter-day Saint ones, argue its grammar means the opposite. The strain shows at Solomon. No text anywhere authorises Solomon's wives; Jacob condemns them and so does 1 Kings 11. Yet D&C 132:38 lists Solomon among those who sinned not. The rule-plus-exception reading keeps the texts formally consistent, at the price of making an "abominable" practice something God can grant. Narrowed, not removed.

unchangeable-god-vs-king-follett.response: Three replies. Blake Ostler and FAIR argue Moroni 8:18 is about God's moral character — he is not partial or fickle — not about his history. The surrounding verses are about God's fairness to children, so reading ontology into it is proof-texting. Second, "from all eternity to all eternity" can be a Hebrew way of saying "throughout all the ages of this creation," which is compatible with a being who existed eternally and attained exaltation before this creation began. Third, since attaining godhood he is unchangeable in everything that matters for salvation, which is all Mormon 9 needs for its argument about miracles.
unchangeable-god-vs-king-follett.rationale: The character-only reading is hard to sustain. Moroni 8:18 and Mormon 9:9 use time-and-being language, and it is the same formula the Bible uses of God's eternal deity in Psalm 90:2. The Book of Mormon nowhere hints that God was once a mortal man. And the King Follett sermon frames the 1844 teaching as overturning the older view — which is exactly the view the 1829 text holds. The idiom-and-cycles reply is speculative and after the fact, with no support in Latter-day Saint scripture. Here the Book of Mormon sides with the Bible against later Mormonism, and that has not been answered.

no-postmortem-repentance.response: Three replies. Amulek is addressing the Zoramites — people who had the gospel and rejected it. His warning applies to them, not to the billions who never heard, and D&C 138:32-34 limits postmortem acceptance to "those who died without a knowledge of this gospel." So the two texts divide humanity without overlap. Second, Latter-day Saint teaching holds that character carries over after death, so this is no easy second chance and Amulek's urgency still stands. Third, 1 Peter 3:19 and 4:6 have Christ preaching to spirits in prison, and 1 Corinthians 15:29 mentions baptism for the dead — so the later doctrine has biblical footing.
no-postmortem-repentance.rationale: The audience-partition answer is internally coherent, it is the church's actual teaching, and critics who ignore it are overclaiming. It does strain the text. Amulek's language is universal in form — "this life is the time for men to prepare" and "the final state of the wicked." The Book of Mormon repeats that scheme elsewhere without the carve-out. And the whole apparatus of spirit prison, proxy ordinances and three degrees of glory is absent from a book whose picture of the next life is simply heaven or hell. As evidence of doctrine developing between 1829 and Nauvoo it holds. As a strict contradiction it can be answered.

born-at-jerusalem.response: Three replies, and this is one of the better sets. The verse says "at Jerusalem which is the land of our forefathers" — land, not city. The Book of Mormon uses "land of Jerusalem" more than forty times for the whole region Lehi left, and its writers were six centuries and an ocean away from Judean village geography. Second, that phrasing is genuinely ancient: Amarna letter EA 287, from the fourteenth century BC, speaks of towns of the land of Jerusalem, and a Dead Sea Scroll fragment says Jeremiah was taken captive from the land of Jerusalem. Neither was knowable in 1829. Third, Bethlehem is five miles away, well inside any such land.
born-at-jerusalem.rationale: This is among the stronger Latter-day Saint replies in the whole section, and Christians should say so plainly. The verse's own wording, the consistent land-versus-city usage, and the genuinely ancient parallels give it real footing. The counters keep some bite — the parallels are regional usages in other contexts, and a nineteenth-century writer being loose explains the same data. Neither side closes it. Note also that even on the critical reading this is an imprecision, not a doctrinal conflict, which is why it is graded low.

plain-precious-things-removed.response: Three replies. Scripture Central and FAIR move the loss earlier — into the first and second centuries, before our earliest substantial manuscripts, most complete New Testament codices being fourth century. If it happened then, uniform later copies cannot rule it out, and they cite Bart Ehrman on early theologically motivated changes. Second, the loss need not be deletion at all: 1 Nephi 13 mentions covenants as well as plain and precious things, so it could mean lost books the Bible itself names, lost ordinances, or lost interpretive keys. Third, the Dead Sea Scrolls show real fluidity in transmission — variant editions of Jeremiah and Samuel.
plain-precious-things-removed.rationale: The manuscript evidence decisively refutes the popular form of this claim — a post-apostolic purge of doctrines out of the Bible's text. The Dead Sea Scrolls close the Old Testament gap, and New Testament transmission is too early, too spread out and too widely attested for a coordinated excision to leave no trace. The sophisticated version survives, but only by retreating to where evidence is thinnest, and by becoming unfalsifiable. It cannot be refuted. It also abandons the natural reading of 1 Nephi 13 and offers nothing positive in its place.

no-nephite-material-culture.response: Five replies, and one of them is a genuine hit. John Sorenson's limited-geography model confines the story to a corridor of about 500 miles in Mesoamerica, so hemisphere-wide absence is beside the point; he lists over 400 claimed correspondences. Second, identification may be impossible in principle: only Maya script is confidently read, and the conquest erased most ancient place-names. Third, John Clark counts about 60 concrete things the text asserts and reckons archaeological support rose from 13% in 1842 to 75% by 2005. Fourth — and this is the strong one — the NHM altars from Yemen, dated to the seventh or sixth century BC, sit on the right bearing for Lehi's route. Fifth, FAIR notes the famous Smithsonian statement was a form letter to reduce mail, not a research finding.
no-nephite-material-culture.rationale: The reply explains why we would not find a signpost saying Zarahemla. It does not answer the harder version. The text asserts a literate civilization with Old World crops, metallurgy and writing, and no material assemblage of that kind exists anywhere in the Americas — finding one would not require reading a place-name. Clark's tally is generic, since warfare, thrones and cities are true of almost any complex society. NHM is a real hit, but it is in Arabia, where the story overlaps documented geography; it says nothing about the two-thirds of the book set in the New World. And the limited-geography model is a retreat from the hemispheric reading Joseph Smith and every nineteenth-century leader held.

translation-seer-stone.response: Four replies, and the first is decisive. The church now teaches this openly — in the Gospel Topics essay, the Joseph Smith Papers, the Saints volumes, and the 2015 photographs in the Ensign. The sources were published in the nineteenth century and discussed in BYU Studies long before the internet found them, so there was no suppression. Second, "Urim and Thummim" was used loosely at the time to cover both the Nephite interpreters and the single stone, which makes the older telling imprecise rather than false. Third, the method is theologically beside the point: if revelation is real, the instrument is incidental, and the Bible has comparable objects. Fourth, Skousen and Carmack argue the dictation was tightly controlled, which the seer-stone account supports.
translation-seer-stone.rationale: On the historical question the church has fully conceded, and the concession is now in official curriculum. Nobody disputes the facts any more. Two things remain, and both are interpretive rather than evidential. The plates were functionally unnecessary to the translation, which sits oddly beside the elaborate story of their retrieval and angelic custody. And the same stone Joseph used for treasure-seeking became the instrument of scripture, which is a fact about where the practice came from. The criticism as usually told — that the method was hidden — is now answered.
